 ‘Minimum wage is not a livable wage’: Barrie workers feel the limits of Ontario’s latest increase
 Ontario raised the minimum wage to $17.95 an hour on Oct. 1, but workers and a local business owner say the increase does little to close the gap with the rising cost of living.
 By Rosemary Jaramillo Barrie Advance 
 Oct 18, 2026 
 Sunday, October 18, 2026 
 1 min to read

 For MJ Molato, Ontario’s latest minimum-wage increase offers a little extra breathing room, but not enough to ease the pressure of rising living costs.
 Ontario’s minimum wage rose from $17.60 to $17.95 an hour on Oct. 1. Simcoe.com asked minimum wage workers in the community about this increase and whether they can keep pace with everyday expenses.
 The Jake’s Bakes employee recently moved into an apartment with his father, with each splitting the rent each month.
 ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW 
 With housing taking a substantial portion of their income, the additional 35 cents an hour has made only a small difference and rising prices can quickly offset the gain.
 “If prices do keep increasing, it kind of just balances out where it kind of feels like there’s no changing at all,” he said.
 ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW 
 That sentiment is shared by other workers in the community.
 Another Barrie worker, Princes Dequilla, said the increase was something to be happy about, but difficult to notice in everyday life.
 ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW 
 “To be honest, I couldn’t really feel that it increased,” Dequilla said.
 ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW
 Although the additional income helps somewhat, it has not solved the pressure of managing bills and other costs.
 “I have a fixed rent, and then I have bills to pay, and I like to shop a lot, too,” she said. “The increase helps, but not that much.”
 One business owner can see the challenges from both sides.
 Jacob Johnson, owner of Jake’s Bakes, said the increase is manageable for his business.
 Johnson said he generally adjusts prices, typically by five or 10 cents at a time, to help account for rising costs. As wages increase, businesses also may need to adjust prices to cover additional expenses, he said.
 Johnson, who previously worked as an employee himself, said small businesses must balance compensating staff fairly with the cost of doing business.
 ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW 
 “I would say the cost of living has exponentially outpaced the minimum wage,” Johnson said.
 Johnson said he would like to see a larger annual increase than 30 or 40 cents an hour.
 “Minimum wage is not a livable wage,” he said.
